comment:
I am concerned with this administration’s attempt to dismantle the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA).

NEPA is the people’s environmental law. It gives communities the opportunity to have a voice in projects that impact their communities, health, and lives. NEPA helps communities protect their access to clean air, clean water, and land free from pollution and contaminants.

These recent actions undercut recent changes to NEPA that brought greater certainty to the process. Eliminating CEQ’s regulations and relying on the interpretation of each individual federal agency involved in NEPA implementation will only cause chaos and further prolong project approvals.

Simultaneously prohibiting federal agencies from considering environmental justice in the NEPA process will further entrench pollution in some of our most vulnerable communities while failing to ensure our infrastructure is resilient in the face of numerous climate threats.

Eliminating all rules that implement NEPA won’t improve decision-making or make the government more effective-especially as the Trump administration fires large numbers of federal workers from the agencies tasked with implementation.

When governments are required to engage with communities and analyze and disclose foreseeable impacts of projects, all of us benefit.

Sincerely,
Simone Fonseca
Victorville, CA

comment:
Council on Environmental Quality
Docket number CEQ-2025-0002

Dear Acting Chair Scarlett:

I am strongly opposed to the interim final rule issued by the Council on Environmental Quality that will rescind 50 years' worth of regulations that implement the National Environmental Policy Act. This recission will upend established case law, policies and procedure and sow great uncertainty among federal agencies, industry, and local communities. I urge you to keep the current CEQ regulations in place.

NEPA was passed by Congress with overwhelming bipartisan support and signed into law by President Nixon in 1970. This statute is our country's basic charter for the protection of the environment, and one of the most important environmental laws in the United States. Since 1978, this vital statute has been implemented through the CEQ's regulations, which have provided clear direction to over 80 federal agencies, tribes, project sponsors, courts, impacted communities, and the broader public. The rescission of these regulations forces these entities to depend on agency-specific NEPA interpretations, which will cause confusion, delays, and litigation.

Concerningly, in guidance issued with the interim final rule, the CEQ urged agencies to use the controversial 2020 regulations issued during the first Trump administration, which were largely reversed by the Biden administration. These regulations were inconsistent with both the letter and spirit of the law; they undermined informed agency decision-making, reduced transparency, and limited critical public involvement, thus denying the public the democratic process at the heart of NEPA. Decisions on certain projects were allowed to move forward without full consideration of their environmental impacts and without a requirement that a broad range of safer, more ecologically sound alternatives be considered.

The interim final rule will cause NEPA processes to be more unpredictable, reducing the public's ability to fully raise concerns about the destruction of wildlife habitat and loss of biodiversity, declines in air and water quality, and harm to public health. I urge you to withdraw this rule.
title: Comment from forman, fay

comment:
Of all things AMERICAN, and directly related to health and our futures, nothing is more important. I oppose the proposed rule withdrawing CEQ's National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) implementing regulations. CEQ's NEPA regulations provide certainty to project sponsors, impacted communities, and over 85 federal agencies. By requiring implementing regulations from each agency, this rule will delay projects, increase compliance costs, reduce transparency, and worsen environmental outcomes for birds and communities.

I have serious concerns about removing the requirement to assess cumulative impacts, which is firmly rooted in the statutory text of NEPA. Without this analysis, agencies may make decisions which on their own do not pose serious environmental risks, but taken together are environmentally detrimental. This change undermines consideration of project contributions to large-scale environmental problems, like climate change or deforestation. With 3 billion birds lost from North America in the last 50 years and nearly two-thirds at risk from climate change, this is no time to ignore the effects of decisions. Any rule barring cumulative analysis is unlawful.

This rule limits consideration of project impacts on communities who are adjacent or downwind of proposed projects, which will reduce public input and result in adverse effects for families, communities, and Tribes, running afoul of the principles affirmed in NEPA.

Finally, I am deeply concerned about allowing private entities to prepare environmental review documents without sufficient oversight. This will reduce the objectivity of environmental reviews, threatening birds and critical ecosystems.

NEPA is a bedrock environmental law that informs science-based, transparent, and accountable decision-making. This proposed rule would weaken those vital standards. Thank you for considering my comments.

comment:
This comment is for the general public as well as the legislators reviewing this. If you are unfamiliar with NEPA, let me go over what it is and why removing this from the Federal Register is a terrible idea.

What NEPA does is require federal agencies to determine if their proposed actions, mainly related to construction and industrial activities but can be related to military actions as well, will have an environmental impact and how much of an impact it will have. This includes:

1.) endangered species
2.) potential pollution
3.) long term effects (including things such as climate change and environmental justice issues, but, speaking as someone who works very closely with NEPA, we have been instructed to not say those things anymore.)
4.) public health
5.) sustainability (also currently discouraged to talk about under the current leadership)

And much more! It forces agencies to consider, though not necessarily adopt, less impactful solutions including the "no action" solution and encourages if not outright demands them to justify why the impact they are causing is necessary. It also aides in the mitigation of harm that may be incurred during the action.

It gives the public the ability to see and comment on all environmental actions, giving transparency to the populace.

The current administration is putting this out there as a cost cutting action. In reality, this will increase costs long term. Public health risks will increase, burdening a community. Mistakes will be more prevalent due to less planning. Law suits against the government will be more common, with the price tag coming out of your tax dollars.

NEPA is a safeguard that both streamlines environmental compliance by sending it to one place instead of multiple different divisions of agencies as well assures that progress comes without jeopardizing future environmental and public health. Repealing NEPA does not just come at the cost of the environment, but the cost of public health and long term taxpayer dollars. This should not be a partisan issue. This is about public health. Keep NEPA in place. Protect our future.

Protecting the vulnerable is how we show strength.

comment:
Council on Environmental Quality
Docket number CEQ-2025-0002

Dear Acting Chair Scarlett:

I am strongly opposed to the interim final rule issued by the Council on Environmental Quality that will rescind 50 years' worth of regulations that implement the National Environmental Policy Act. This recission will upend established case law, policies and procedure and sow great uncertainty among federal agencies, industry, and local communities. I urge you to keep the current CEQ regulations in place.

NEPA was passed by Congress with overwhelming bipartisan support and signed into law by President Nixon in 1970. This statute is our country's basic charter for the protection of the environment, and one of the most important environmental laws in the United States. Since 1978, this vital statute has been implemented through the CEQ's regulations, which have provided clear direction to over 80 federal agencies, tribes, project sponsors, courts, impacted communities, and the broader public. The rescission of these regulations forces these entities to depend on agency-specific NEPA interpretations, which will cause confusion, delays, and litigation.

Concerningly, in guidance issued with the interim final rule, the CEQ urged agencies to use the controversial 2020 regulations issued during the first Trump administration, which were largely reversed by the Biden administration. These regulations were inconsistent with both the letter and spirit of the law; they undermined informed agency decision-making, reduced transparency, and limited critical public involvement, thus denying the public the democratic process at the heart of NEPA. Decisions on certain projects were allowed to move forward without full consideration of their environmental impacts and without a requirement that a broad range of safer, more ecologically sound alternatives be considered.

The interim final rule will cause NEPA processes to be more unpredictable, reducing the public's ability to fully raise concerns about the destruction of wildlife habitat and loss of biodiversity, declines in air and water quality, and harm to public health. I urge you to withdraw this rule.

comment:
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the interim decision for the Removal of National Environmental Policy Act Implementing Regulations.

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed removal of the Council on Environmental Quality’s (CEQ) National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) implementing regulations. This action would be a significant rollback of environmental protections, weakening and confusing the framework that ensures federal agencies conduct meaningful environmental reviews before approving projects that may have significant environmental, cultural, and socio-economic impacts.

For over five decades, NEPA has been instrumental in safeguarding both human health and the integrity of our ecosystems in the United States. NEPA and its associated regulations have been used to protect our public land and forests, stopped highway projects from further fragmenting and polluting communities that least deserve it, and more often than not, simply improved big development projects by requiring us to take a closer look at what was being proposed and offering better alternatives.

This federal agency coordination that is laid out in the CEQ NEPA regulations saves taxpayers millions of dollars every year by preventing bad projects from getting approved before better alternatives are considered. Without the highest standards of transparency and coordination required by NEPA, and enshrined in the CEQ NEPA regulations, federal agency approval of large projects will likely be clouded in community suspicion and will be much more likely to attract litigation under the NEPA statute.

The CEQ NEPA regulations are justified as necessary tools for coordination among federal agencies and Federally Recognized Indian Tribes. Tribes have signed nearly 400 treaties with the U.S. government and all of these place cross-cutting duties on federal agencies to work together to respect and uphold these treaty obligations, which are the supreme law of the land under the Constitution’s Supremacy Clause. In addition, the U.S. government has a trust responsibility to tribal members and tribal governments. By removing the regulations, CEQ neglects these duties and doesn’t give the agencies the structure they need to coordinate their treaty-based obligations throughout ceded and unceded lands and waters.

NEPA has been a cornerstone of environmental protections for decades, and the CEQ NEPA regulations are a huge part of that success. The effectiveness of this policy has cascaded throughout the world. More than 80 countries have adopted policies based on the establishment and implementation of NEPA in the United States. The United States' created a powerful path for the world to embark on, but now we risk undermining that legacy by stripping away these protections. Backsliding on NEPA implementation and transparent environmental review which will be setting a dangerously misguided precedent for the planet. Eliminating these procedures will greatly undermine our collective ability to safeguard the planet from the environmental damage associated with extraction while enabling corporations to devastate our ecosystems without anyone fully grasping or mitigating the consequences.

Sincerely,

comment:
Council on Environmental Quality
Docket number CEQ-2025-0002

Dear Acting Chair Scarlett:

I am strongly opposed to the interim final rule issued by the Council on Environmental Quality that will rescind 50 years' worth of regulations that implement the National Environmental Policy Act. This recission will upend established case law, policies and procedure and sow great uncertainty among federal agencies, industry, and local communities. I urge you to keep the current CEQ regulations in place.

NEPA was passed by Congress with overwhelming bipartisan support and signed into law by President Nixon in 1970. This statute is our country's basic charter for the protection of the environment, and one of the most important environmental laws in the United States. Since 1978, this vital statute has been implemented through the CEQ's regulations, which have provided clear direction to over 80 federal agencies, tribes, project sponsors, courts, impacted communities, and the broader public. The rescission of these regulations forces these entities to depend on agency-specific NEPA interpretations, which will cause confusion, delays, and litigation.

Concerningly, in guidance issued with the interim final rule, the CEQ urged agencies to use the controversial 2020 regulations issued during the first Trump administration, which were largely reversed by the Biden administration. These regulations were inconsistent with both the letter and spirit of the law; they undermined informed agency decision-making, reduced transparency, and limited critical public involvement, thus denying the public the democratic process at the heart of NEPA. Decisions on certain projects were allowed to move forward without full consideration of their environmental impacts and without a requirement that a broad range of safer, more ecologically sound alternatives be considered.

The interim final rule will cause NEPA processes to be more unpredictable, reducing the public's ability to fully raise concerns about the destruction of wildlife habitat and loss of biodiversity, declines in air and water quality, and harm to public health. I urge you to withdraw this rule.

comment:
Council on Environmental Quality
Docket number CEQ-2025-0002

Dear Acting Chair Scarlett:

I am strongly opposed to the interim final rule issued by the Council on Environmental Quality that will rescind 50 years' worth of regulations that implement the National Environmental Policy Act. This recission will upend established case law, policies and procedure and sow great uncertainty among federal agencies, industry, and local communities. I urge you to keep the current CEQ regulations in place.

NEPA was passed by Congress with overwhelming bipartisan support and signed into law by President Nixon in 1970. This statute is our country's basic charter for the protection of the environment, and one of the most important environmental laws in the United States. Since 1978, this vital statute has been implemented through the CEQ's regulations, which have provided clear direction to over 80 federal agencies, tribes, project sponsors, courts, impacted communities, and the broader public. The rescission of these regulations forces these entities to depend on agency-specific NEPA interpretations, which will cause confusion, delays, and litigation.

Concerningly, in guidance issued with the interim final rule, the CEQ urged agencies to use the controversial 2020 regulations issued during the first Trump administration, which were largely reversed by the Biden administration. These regulations were inconsistent with both the letter and spirit of the law; they undermined informed agency decision-making, reduced transparency, and limited critical public involvement, thus denying the public the democratic process at the heart of NEPA. Decisions on certain projects were allowed to move forward without full consideration of their environmental impacts and without a requirement that a broad range of safer, more ecologically sound alternatives be considered.

The interim final rule will cause NEPA processes to be more unpredictable, reducing the public's ability to fully raise concerns about the destruction of wildlife habitat and loss of biodiversity, declines in air and water quality, and harm to public health. I urge you to withdraw this rule.

comment:
Council on Environmental Quality
Docket number CEQ-2025-0002

Dear Acting Chair Scarlett:

I am strongly opposed to the interim final rule issued by the Council on Environmental Quality that will rescind 50 years' worth of regulations that implement the National Environmental Policy Act. This recission will upend established case law, policies and procedure and sow great uncertainty among federal agencies, industry, and local communities. I urge you to keep the current CEQ regulations in place.

NEPA was passed by Congress with overwhelming bipartisan support and signed into law by President Nixon in 1970. This statute is our country's basic charter for the protection of the environment, and one of the most important environmental laws in the United States. Since 1978, this vital statute has been implemented through the CEQ's regulations, which have provided clear direction to over 80 federal agencies, tribes, project sponsors, courts, impacted communities, and the broader public. The rescission of these regulations forces these entities to depend on agency-specific NEPA interpretations, which will cause confusion, delays, and litigation.

Concerningly, in guidance issued with the interim final rule, the CEQ urged agencies to use the controversial 2020 regulations issued during the first Trump administration, which were largely reversed by the Biden administration. These regulations were inconsistent with both the letter and spirit of the law; they undermined informed agency decision-making, reduced transparency, and limited critical public involvement, thus denying the public the democratic process at the heart of NEPA. Decisions on certain projects were allowed to move forward without full consideration of their environmental impacts and without a requirement that a broad range of safer, more ecologically sound alternatives be considered.

The interim final rule will cause NEPA processes to be more unpredictable, reducing the public's ability to fully raise concerns about the destruction of wildlife habitat and loss of biodiversity, declines in air and water quality, and harm to public health. I urge you to withdraw this rule.

My name [and health credentials if relevant] is _____, and I would like to express my strong opposition to the Council on Environmental Quality’s interim final rule, Removal of National Environmental Policy Act Implementing Regulations, Docket No. CEQ-2025-0002.

[Include some or all of the following points:]
The National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) is a foundational law that protects the environment from unnecessary degradation, and allows public input on major federal projects, such as the development of pipelines and highways. Through the application of NEPA, many communities have advocated for themselves and avoided poor health outcomes and other safety concerns associated with environmental harms.

Community engagement and buy-in from community members is critical to any project that has the potential to impact the environment and the health of residents.

Local residents deserve to know the risks that a proposed project would pose. It is the duty of the federal government under NEPA to communicate this information in an understandable and accessible manner. Increased transparency between the federal government and local communities creates a shared understanding and benefits all parties involved.

Environmental injustice is real and must be acknowledged through the NEPA process. Low-income communities and people of color are disproportionately burdened by environmental impacts and the adverse health outcomes associated with them. Removing the consideration of cumulative impacts will cause additional risk to those most vulnerable.

While there have been many attempts to streamline NEPA by past administrations, this action will not improve the process or lead to improved government efficiency. Rather, it would allow projects to be completed at the cost of our environment, health, and sense of community.

comment:
Council on Environmental Quality
Docket number CEQ-2025-0002

Dear Acting Chair Scarlett:

I am strongly opposed to the interim final rule issued by the Council on Environmental Quality that will rescind 50 years' worth of regulations that implement the National Environmental Policy Act. This recission will upend established case law, policies and procedure and sow great uncertainty among federal agencies, industry, and local communities. I urge you to keep the current CEQ regulations in place.

NEPA was passed by Congress with overwhelming bipartisan support and signed into law by President Nixon in 1970. This statute is our country's basic charter for the protection of the environment, and one of the most important environmental laws in the United States. Since 1978, this vital statute has been implemented through the CEQ's regulations, which have provided clear direction to over 80 federal agencies, tribes, project sponsors, courts, impacted communities, and the broader public. The rescission of these regulations forces these entities to depend on agency-specific NEPA interpretations, which will cause confusion, delays, and litigation.

Concerningly, in guidance issued with the interim final rule, the CEQ urged agencies to use the controversial 2020 regulations issued during the first Trump administration, which were largely reversed by the Biden administration. These regulations were inconsistent with both the letter and spirit of the law; they undermined informed agency decision-making, reduced transparency, and limited critical public involvement, thus denying the public the democratic process at the heart of NEPA. Decisions on certain projects were allowed to move forward without full consideration of their environmental impacts and without a requirement that a broad range of safer, more ecologically sound alternatives be considered.

The interim final rule will cause NEPA processes to be more unpredictable, reducing the public's ability to fully raise concerns about the destruction of wildlife habitat and loss of biodiversity, declines in air and water quality, and harm to public health. I urge you to withdraw this rule.

I am from Ely, MN, an area that heavily relies on natural resources AND tourism for our income. Our area and livelihoods have been threatened many times by businesses and corporations that wanted to destroy our water and/or land. NEPA has provided the means to protect us. So thank you for the opportunity to comment on the interim decision for the Removal of National Environmental Policy Act Implementing Regulations.

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed removal of the Council on Environmental Quality’s (CEQ) National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) implementing regulations. This action would be a significant rollback of environmental protections, weakening and confusing the framework that ensures federal agencies conduct meaningful environmental reviews before approving projects that may have significant environmental, cultural, and socio-economic impacts.

For over 50 years, NEPA has safeguarded human health and our ecosystems. NEPA and its associated regulations have been used to protect our public land and forests, stopped highway projects from further fragmenting and polluting communities that least deserve it, and more often than not, simply improved big development projects by requiring us to take a closer look at what was being proposed and offering better alternatives.

This federal agency coordination that is laid out in the CEQ NEPA regulations saves taxpayers millions of dollars every year by preventing bad projects from getting approved before better alternatives are considered. Without the highest standards of transparency and coordination required by NEPA, and enshrined in the CEQ NEPA regulations, federal agency approval of large projects will likely be clouded in community suspicion and will be much more likely to attract litigation under the NEPA statute.

The CEQ NEPA regulations are justified as necessary tools for coordination among federal agencies and Federally Recognized Indian Tribes. Tribes have signed nearly 400 treaties with the U.S. government and all of these place cross-cutting duties on federal agencies to work together to respect and uphold these treaty obligations, which are the supreme law of the land under the Constitution’s Supremacy Clause. In addition, the U.S. government has a trust responsibility to tribal members and tribal governments. By removing the regulations, CEQ neglects these duties and doesn’t give the agencies the structure they need to coordinate their treaty-based obligations throughout ceded and unceded lands and waters.

NEPA has been a cornerstone of environmental protections for decades, and the CEQ NEPA regulations are a huge part of that success. The effectiveness of this policy has cascaded throughout the world. More than 80 countries have adopted policies based on the establishment and implementation of NEPA in the United States. The United States' created a powerful path for the world to embark on, but now we risk undermining that legacy by stripping away these protections. Backsliding on NEPA implementation and transparent environmental review which will be setting a dangerously misguided precedent for the planet. Eliminating these procedures will greatly undermine our collective ability to safeguard the planet from the environmental damage associated with extraction while enabling corporations to devastate our ecosystems without anyone fully grasping or mitigating the consequences.

This recission will upend established case law, policies and procedure and sow great uncertainty among federal agencies, industry, and local communities. I urge you to keep the current CEQ regulations in place.

NEPA was passed by Congress with overwhelming bipartisan support and signed into law by President Nixon in 1970. This statute is our country's basic charter for the protection of the environment, and one of the most important environmental laws in the United States. Since 1978, this vital statute has been implemented through the CEQ's regulations, which have provided clear direction to over 80 federal agencies, tribes, project sponsors, courts, impacted communities, and the broader public. The rescission of these regulations forces these entities to depend on agency-specific NEPA interpretations, which will cause confusion, delays, and litigation.

Concerningly, in guidance issued with the interim final rule, the CEQ urged agencies to use the controversial 2020 regulations issued during the first Trump administration, which were largely reversed by the Biden administration. These regulations were inconsistent with both the letter and spirit of the law; they undermined informed agency decision-making, reduced transparency, and limited critical public involvement, thus denying the public the democratic process at the heart of NEPA. Decisions on certain projects were allowed to move forward without full consideration of their environmental impacts and without a requirement that a broad range of safer, more ecologically sound alternatives be considered.

The interim final rule will cause NEPA processes to be more unpredictable, reducing the public's ability to fully raise concerns about the destruction of wildlife habitat and loss of biodiversity, declines in air and water quality, and harm to public health. I urge you to withdraw this rule.
title: Comment from Mitchell, David

comment:
I am concerned with this administration’s attempt to dismantle the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA).

NEPA is the people’s environmental law. It gives communities the opportunity to have a voice in projects that impact their communities, health, and lives. NEPA helps communities protect their access to clean air, clean water, and land free from pollution and contaminants.

These recent actions undercut recent changes to NEPA that brought greater certainty to the process. Eliminating CEQ’s regulations and relying on the interpretation of each individual federal agency involved in NEPA implementation will only cause chaos and further prolong project approvals.

Simultaneously prohibiting federal agencies from considering environmental justice in the NEPA process will further entrench pollution in some of our most vulnerable communities while failing to ensure our infrastructure is resilient in the face of numerous climate threats.

Eliminating all rules that implement NEPA won’t improve decision-making or make the government more effective-especially as the Trump administration fires large numbers of federal workers from the agencies tasked with implementation.

When governments are required to engage with communities and analyze and disclose foreseeable impacts of projects, all of us benefit.

Sincerely,
Angela Spangler
Riverside, CA
title: Comment from Spangler, Angela

comment:
I oppose the proposed rule withdrawing CEQ's National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) implementing regulations. CEQ's NEPA regulations provide certainty to project sponsors, impacted communities, and over 85 federal agencies. By requiring implementing regulations from each agency, this rule will delay projects, increase compliance costs, reduce transparency, and worsen environmental outcomes for birds and communities.

I have serious concerns about removing the requirement to assess cumulative impacts, which is firmly rooted in the statutory text of NEPA. Without this analysis, agencies may make decisions which on their own do not pose serious environmental risks, but taken together are environmentally detrimental. This change undermines consideration of project contributions to large-scale environmental problems, like climate change or deforestation. With 3 billion birds lost from North America in the last 50 years and nearly two-thirds at risk from climate change, this is no time to ignore the effects of decisions. Any rule barring cumulative analysis is unlawful.

This rule limits consideration of project impacts on communities who are adjacent or downwind of proposed projects, which will reduce public input and result in adverse effects for families, communities, and Tribes, running afoul of the principles affirmed in NEPA.

Finally, I am deeply concerned about allowing private entities to prepare environmental review documents without sufficient oversight. This will reduce the objectivity of environmental reviews, threatening birds and critical ecosystems.

NEPA is a bedrock environmental law that informs science-based, transparent, and accountable decision-making. This proposed rule would weaken those vital standards. Thank you for considering my comments.

NEPA was passed by Congress with overwhelming bipartisan support and signed into law by President Nixon in 1970. This statute is our country's basic charter for the protection of the environment, and one of the most important environmental laws in the United States. Since 1978, this vital statute has been implemented through the CEQ's regulations, which have provided clear direction to over 80 federal agencies, tribes, project sponsors, courts, impacted communities, and the broader public. The rescission of these regulations forces these entities to depend on agency-specific NEPA interpretations, which will cause confusion, delays, and litigation.

Concerningly, in guidance issued with the interim final rule, the CEQ urged agencies to use the controversial 2020 regulations issued during the first Trump administration, which were largely reversed by the Biden administration. These regulations were inconsistent with both the letter and spirit of the law; they undermined informed agency decision-making, reduced transparency, and limited critical public involvement, thus denying the public the democratic process at the heart of NEPA. Decisions on certain projects were allowed to move forward without full consideration of their environmental impacts and without a requirement that a broad range of safer, more ecologically sound alternatives be considered.

The interim final rule will cause NEPA processes to be more unpredictable, reducing the public's ability to fully raise concerns about the destruction of wildlife habitat and loss of biodiversity, declines in air and water quality, and harm to public health. I urge you to withdraw this rule.

I strongly oppose CEQ’s decision to rescind the 1978 NEPA regulations — a set of rules that have been respected and followed by every administration, Republican and Democrat, for nearly 50 years. These regulations didn’t block projects — they simply ensured that environmental consequences were considered, safer alternatives explored, and the public had a right to know what was happening to their air, water, and land.

CEQ’s authority to set uniform environmental review standards has been upheld for decades — and respected by Presidents from Nixon to Reagan to both Bushes. This isn’t about legality — it’s about dismantling environmental protections to benefit corporate polluters.

Abandoning these protections and handing environmental oversight directly to agencies now led by industry insiders will gut accountability, silence public input, and leave your own children and grandchildren with a weaker, degraded America — a country incapable of protecting its own natural heritage. The air they breathe, the water they drink, the landscapes that define this nation — you are trading all of it away for short-term profit.

As Theodore Roosevelt said:
“Of all the questions which can come before this nation…there is none which compares in importance with the great central task of leaving this land even a better land for our descendants than it is for us.”

I urge CEQ to abandon this disastrous rollback and preserve the 1978 NEPA regulations in full. History — and your own descendants — will judge your choice.
Sincerely,
Tim Gibson
Dallas, TX

Community engagement and buy-in from community members is critical to any project that has the potential to impact the environment and the health of residents.

Local residents deserve to know the risks that a proposed project would pose. Increased transparency between the federal government and local communities creates a shared understanding and benefits all parties involved.

Environmental injustice is real and must be acknowledged through the NEPA process. Low-income communities and people of color are disproportionately burdened by environmental impacts and the adverse health outcomes associated with them. Removing the consideration of cumulative impacts will cause additional risk to those most vulnerable.

While there have been many attempts to streamline NEPA by past administrations, this action will not improve the process or lead to improved government efficiency. Rather, it would allow projects to be completed at the cost of our environment, health, and sense of community.

This interim final rule is insufficient in protecting both the environment and health, which contradicts the mission that the Council on Environmental Quality was tasked with. NEPA should not be weakened as any attempt to do so would put vulnerable communities at risk of environmental degradation and health harms.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment.

Ms. Ellen Rosenblum

The interim final rule will cause NEPA processes to be more unpredictable, reducing the public's ability to fully raise concerns about the destruction of wildlife habitat and loss of biodiversity, declines in air and water quality, and harm to public health. I urge you to withdraw this rule.

comment:
Council on Environmental Quality
Docket number CEQ-2025-0002

Dear Acting Chair Scarlett:

I am strongly opposed to the interim final rule issued by the Council on Environmental Quality that will rescind 50 years' worth of regulations that implement the National Environmental Policy Act. This recission will upend established case law, policies and procedure and sow great uncertainty among federal agencies, industry, and local communities. I urge you to keep the current CEQ regulations in place.

NEPA was passed by Congress with overwhelming bipartisan support and signed into law by President Nixon in 1970. This statute is our country's basic charter for the protection of the environment, and one of the most important environmental laws in the United States. Since 1978, this vital statute has been implemented through the CEQ's regulations, which have provided clear direction to over 80 federal agencies, tribes, project sponsors, courts, impacted communities, and the broader public. The rescission of these regulations forces these entities to depend on agency-specific NEPA interpretations, which will cause confusion, delays, and litigation.

Concerningly, in guidance issued with the interim final rule, the CEQ urged agencies to use the controversial 2020 regulations issued during the first Trump administration, which were largely reversed by the Biden administration. These regulations were inconsistent with both the letter and spirit of the law; they undermined informed agency decision-making, reduced transparency, and limited critical public involvement, thus denying the public the democratic process at the heart of NEPA. Decisions on certain projects were allowed to move forward without full consideration of their environmental impacts and without a requirement that a broad range of safer, more ecologically sound alternatives be considered.

The interim final rule will cause NEPA processes to be more unpredictable, reducing the public's ability to fully raise concerns about the destruction of wildlife habitat and loss of biodiversity, declines in air and water quality, and harm to public health. I urge you to withdraw this rule.

comment:
Council on Environmental Quality
Docket number CEQ-2025-0002

Dear Acting Chair Scarlett:

I am strongly opposed to the interim final rule issued by the Council on Environmental Quality that will rescind 50 years' worth of regulations that implement the National Environmental Policy Act. This recission will upend established case law, policies and procedure and sow great uncertainty among federal agencies, industry, and local communities. I urge you to keep the current CEQ regulations in place.

NEPA was passed by Congress with overwhelming bipartisan support and signed into law by President Nixon in 1970. This statute is our country's basic charter for the protection of the environment, and one of the most important environmental laws in the United States. Since 1978, this vital statute has been implemented through the CEQ's regulations, which have provided clear direction to over 80 federal agencies, tribes, project sponsors, courts, impacted communities, and the broader public. The rescission of these regulations forces these entities to depend on agency-specific NEPA interpretations, which will cause confusion, delays, and litigation.

Concerningly, in guidance issued with the interim final rule, the CEQ urged agencies to use the controversial 2020 regulations issued during the first Trump administration, which were largely reversed by the Biden administration. These regulations were inconsistent with both the letter and spirit of the law; they undermined informed agency decision-making, reduced transparency, and limited critical public involvement, thus denying the public the democratic process at the heart of NEPA. Decisions on certain projects were allowed to move forward without full consideration of their environmental impacts and without a requirement that a broad range of safer, more ecologically sound alternatives be considered.

The interim final rule will cause NEPA processes to be more unpredictable, reducing the public's ability to fully raise concerns about the destruction of wildlife habitat and loss of biodiversity, declines in air and water quality, and harm to public health. I urge you to withdraw this rule.

I am concerned with this administration’s attempt to dismantle the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA).

NEPA is the people’s environmental law. It gives communities the opportunity to have a voice in projects that impact their communities, health, and lives. NEPA helps communities protect their access to clean air, clean water, and land free from pollution and contaminants.

These recent actions undercut recent changes to NEPA that brought greater certainty to the process. Eliminating CEQ’s regulations and relying on the interpretation of each individual federal agency involved in NEPA implementation will only cause chaos and further prolong project approvals.

Simultaneously prohibiting federal agencies from considering environmental justice in the NEPA process will further entrench pollution in some of our most vulnerable communities while failing to ensure our infrastructure is resilient in the face of numerous climate threats.

Eliminating all rules that implement NEPA won’t improve decision-making or make the government more effective-especially as the Trump administration fires large numbers of federal workers from the agencies tasked with implementation.

When governments are required to engage with communities and analyze and disclose foreseeable impacts of projects, all of us benefit.

Sincerely,
Daniel Sweeney
Rochester, PA
title: Comment from Sweeney, Daniel

comment:
I oppose the proposed rule withdrawing CEQ's National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) implementing regulations. CEQ's NEPA regulations provide certainty to project sponsors, impacted communities, and over 85 federal agencies. By requiring implementing regulations from each agency, this rule will delay projects, increase compliance costs, reduce transparency, and worsen environmental outcomes for birds and communities.

I have serious concerns about removing the requirement to assess cumulative impacts, which is firmly rooted in the statutory text of NEPA. Without this analysis, agencies may make decisions which on their own do not pose serious environmental risks, but taken together are environmentally detrimental. This change undermines consideration of project contributions to large-scale environmental problems, like climate change or deforestation. With 3 billion birds lost from North America in the last 50 years and nearly two-thirds at risk from climate change, this is no time to ignore the effects of decisions. Any rule barring cumulative analysis is unlawful.

This rule limits consideration of project impacts on communities who are adjacent or downwind of proposed projects, which will reduce public input and result in adverse effects for families, communities, and Tribes, running afoul of the principles affirmed in NEPA.

Finally, I am deeply concerned about allowing private entities to prepare environmental review documents without sufficient oversight. This will reduce the objectivity of environmental reviews, threatening birds and critical ecosystems.

NEPA is a bedrock environmental law that informs science-based, transparent, and accountable decision-making. This proposed rule would weaken those vital standards. Thank you for considering my comments.

NEPA was passed by Congress with overwhelming bipartisan support and signed into law by President Nixon in 1970. This statute is our country's basic charter for the protection of the environment, and one of the most important environmental laws in the United States. Since 1978, this vital statute has been implemented through the CEQ's regulations, which have provided clear direction to over 80 federal agencies, tribes, project sponsors, courts, impacted communities, and the broader public. The rescission of these regulations forces these entities to depend on agency-specific NEPA interpretations, which will cause confusion, delays, and litigation.

Concerningly, in guidance issued with the interim final rule, the CEQ urged agencies to use the controversial 2020 regulations issued during the first Trump administration, which were largely reversed by the Biden administration. These regulations were inconsistent with both the letter and spirit of the law; they undermined informed agency decision-making, reduced transparency, and limited critical public involvement, thus denying the public the democratic process at the heart of NEPA. The interim final rule will cause NEPA processes to be more unpredictable, reducing the public's ability to fully raise concerns about the destruction of wildlife habitat and loss of biodiversity, declines in air and water quality, and harm to public health. I urge you to withdraw this rule.

comment:
Council on Environmental Quality
Docket number CEQ-2025-0002

Dear Acting Chair Scarlett:

I am strongly opposed to the interim final rule issued by the Council on Environmental Quality that will rescind 50 years' worth of regulations that implement the National Environmental Policy Act. This recission will upend established case law, policies and procedure and sow great uncertainty among federal agencies, industry, and local communities. I urge you to keep the current CEQ regulations in place.

NEPA was passed by Congress with overwhelming bipartisan support and signed into law by President Nixon in 1970. This statute is our country's basic charter for the protection of the environment, and one of the most important environmental laws in the United States. Since 1978, this vital statute has been implemented through the CEQ's regulations, which have provided clear direction to over 80 federal agencies, tribes, project sponsors, courts, impacted communities, and the broader public. The rescission of these regulations forces these entities to depend on agency-specific NEPA interpretations, which will cause confusion, delays, and litigation.

Concerningly, in guidance issued with the interim final rule, the CEQ urged agencies to use the controversial 2020 regulations issued during the first Trump administration, which were largely reversed by the Biden administration. These regulations were inconsistent with both the letter and spirit of the law; they undermined informed agency decision-making, reduced transparency, and limited critical public involvement, thus denying the public the democratic process at the heart of NEPA. Decisions on certain projects were allowed to move forward without full consideration of their environmental impacts and without a requirement that a broad range of safer, more ecologically sound alternatives be considered.

The interim final rule will cause NEPA processes to be more unpredictable, reducing the public's ability to fully raise concerns about the destruction of wildlife habitat and loss of biodiversity, declines in air and water quality, and harm to public health. I urge you to withdraw this rule.

My name is Ellen Barfield, and I would like to express my VERY strong opposition to the Council on Environmental Quality’s interim final rule, Removal of National Environmental Policy Act Implementing Regulations, Docket No. CEQ-2025-0002.

Removing the consideration of cumulative impacts will cause additional risk to those most vulnerable.

This interim final rule is insufficient in protecting both the environment and health, which contradicts the mission that the Council on Environmental Quality was tasked with. NEPA MUST not be weakened as any attempt to do so would put vulnerable communities at risk of environmental degradation and health harms.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment.

NEPA is the people’s environmental law. It gives communities the opportunity to have a voice in projects that impact their communities, health, and lives. NEPA helps communities protect their access to clean air, clean water, and land free from pollution and contaminants.

These recent actions undercut recent changes to NEPA that brought greater certainty to the process. Eliminating CEQ’s regulations and relying on the interpretation of each individual federal agency involved in NEPA implementation will only cause chaos and further prolong project approvals.

Simultaneously prohibiting federal agencies from considering environmental justice in the NEPA process will further entrench pollution in some of our most vulnerable communities while failing to ensure our infrastructure is resilient in the face of numerous climate threats.

Eliminating all rules that implement NEPA won’t improve decision-making or make the government more effective-especially as the Trump administration fires large numbers of federal workers from the agencies tasked with implementation.

When governments are required to engage with communities and analyze and disclose foreseeable impacts of projects, all of us benefit.

Sincerely,
Daniel Wall
New Egypt, NJ

comment:
I oppose the proposed rule withdrawing CEQ's National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) implementing regulations. CEQ's NEPA regulations provide certainty to project sponsors, impacted communities, and over 85 federal agencies. By requiring implementing regulations from each agency, this rule will delay projects, increase compliance costs, reduce transparency, and worsen environmental outcomes for birds and communities.

I have serious concerns about removing the requirement to assess cumulative impacts, which is firmly rooted in the statutory text of NEPA. Without this analysis, agencies may make decisions which on their own do not pose serious environmental risks, but taken together are environmentally detrimental. This change undermines consideration of project contributions to large-scale environmental problems, like climate change or deforestation. With 3 billion birds lost from North America in the last 50 years and nearly two-thirds at risk from climate change, this is no time to ignore the effects of decisions. Any rule barring cumulative analysis is unlawful.

This rule limits consideration of project impacts on communities who are adjacent or downwind of proposed projects, which will reduce public input and result in adverse effects for families, communities, and Tribes, running afoul of the principles affirmed in NEPA.

Finally, I am deeply concerned about allowing private entities to prepare environmental review documents without sufficient oversight. This will reduce the objectivity of environmental reviews, threatening birds and critical ecosystems.

NEPA is a bedrock environmental law that informs science-based, transparent, and accountable decision-making. This proposed rule would weaken those vital standards. Thank you for considering my comments.

The interim final rule will likewise lead to increased uncertainty, delays, inefficiencies, and other unintended adverse consequences. I strongly urge CEQ to reverse course and resume the necessary work of ensuring that NEPA’s procedural requirements lead to informed decisions that are better for the environment and people, as intended by the statute.

Thank you.

This interim final rule is insufficient in protecting both the environment and health, which contradicts the mission that the Council on Environmental Quality was tasked with. comment:
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the interim decision for the Removal of National Environmental Policy Act Implementing Regulations.

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed removal of the Council on Environmental Quality’s (CEQ) National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) implementing regulations. This action would be a significant rollback of environmental protections, weakening and confusing the framework that ensures federal agencies conduct meaningful environmental reviews before approving projects that may have significant environmental, cultural, and socio-economic impacts.

For over five decades, NEPA has been instrumental in safeguarding both human health and the integrity of our ecosystems in the United States. NEPA and its associated regulations have been used to protect our public land and forests, stopped highway projects from further fragmenting and polluting communities that least deserve it, and more often than not, simply improved big development projects by requiring us to take a closer look at what was being proposed and offering better alternatives.

This federal agency coordination that is laid out in the CEQ NEPA regulations saves taxpayers millions of dollars every year by preventing bad projects from getting approved before better alternatives are considered. Without the highest standards of transparency and coordination required by NEPA, and enshrined in the CEQ NEPA regulations, federal agency approval of large projects will likely be clouded in community suspicion and will be much more likely to attract litigation under the NEPA statute.

The CEQ NEPA regulations are justified as necessary tools for coordination among federal agencies and Federally Recognized Indian Tribes. Tribes have signed nearly 400 treaties with the U.S. government and all of these place cross-cutting duties on federal agencies to work together to respect and uphold these treaty obligations, which are the supreme law of the land under the Constitution’s Supremacy Clause. In addition, the U.S. government has a trust responsibility to tribal members and tribal governments. By removing the regulations, CEQ neglects these duties and doesn’t give the agencies the structure they need to coordinate their treaty-based obligations throughout ceded and unceded lands and waters.

NEPA has been a cornerstone of environmental protections for decades, and the CEQ NEPA regulations are a huge part of that success. The effectiveness of this policy has cascaded throughout the world. More than 80 countries have adopted policies based on the establishment and implementation of NEPA in the United States. The United States' created a powerful path for the world to embark on, but now we risk undermining that legacy by stripping away these protections. Backsliding on NEPA implementation and transparent environmental review which will be setting a dangerously misguided precedent for the planet. Eliminating these procedures will greatly undermine our collective ability to safeguard the planet from the environmental damage associated with extraction while enabling corporations to devastate our ecosystems without anyone fully grasping or mitigating the consequences.

NEPA is the people’s environmental law. It gives communities the opportunity to have a voice in projects that impact their communities, health, and lives. NEPA helps communities protect their access to clean air, clean water, and land free from pollution and contaminants.

These recent actions undercut recent changes to NEPA that brought greater certainty to the process. Eliminating CEQ’s regulations and relying on the interpretation of each individual federal agency involved in NEPA implementation will only cause chaos and further prolong project approvals.

Simultaneously prohibiting federal agencies from considering environmental justice in the NEPA process will further entrench pollution in some of our most vulnerable communities while failing to ensure our infrastructure is resilient in the face of numerous climate threats.

Eliminating all rules that implement NEPA won’t improve decision-making or make the government more effective-especially as the Trump administration fires large numbers of federal workers from the agencies tasked with implementation.

When governments are required to engage with communities and analyze and disclose foreseeable impacts of projects, all of us benefit.

Sincerely,
Erik Hvoslef
Salida, CO
title: Comment from Hvoslef, Erik

comment:
I oppose the proposed rule withdrawing CEQ's National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) implementing regulations. CEQ's NEPA regulations provide certainty to project sponsors, impacted communities, and over 85 federal agencies. By requiring implementing regulations from each agency, this rule will delay projects, increase compliance costs, reduce transparency, and worsen environmental outcomes for birds and communities.

I have serious concerns about removing the requirement to assess cumulative impacts, which is firmly rooted in the statutory text of NEPA. Without this analysis, agencies may make decisions which on their own do not pose serious environmental risks, but taken together are environmentally detrimental. This change undermines consideration of project contributions to large-scale environmental problems, like climate change or deforestation. With 3 billion birds lost from North America in the last 50 years and nearly two-thirds at risk from climate change, this is no time to ignore the effects of decisions. Any rule barring cumulative analysis is unlawful.

This rule limits consideration of project impacts on communities who are adjacent or downwind of proposed projects, which will reduce public input and result in adverse effects for families, communities, and Tribes, running afoul of the principles affirmed in NEPA.

Finally, I am deeply concerned about allowing private entities to prepare environmental review documents without sufficient oversight. This will reduce the objectivity of environmental reviews, threatening birds and critical ecosystems.

NEPA is a bedrock environmental law that informs science-based, transparent, and accountable decision-making. This proposed rule would weaken those vital standards. Thank you for considering my comments.

comment:
Council on Environmental Quality
Docket number CEQ-2025-0002

Dear Acting Chair Scarlett:

I am strongly opposed to the interim final rule issued by the Council on Environmental Quality that will rescind 50 years' worth of regulations that implement the National Environmental Policy Act. This recission will upend established case law, policies and procedure and sow great uncertainty among federal agencies, industry, and local communities. I urge you to keep the current CEQ regulations in place.

NEPA was passed by Congress with overwhelming bipartisan support and signed into law by President Nixon in 1970. This statute is our country's basic charter for the protection of the environment, and one of the most important environmental laws in the United States. Since 1978, this vital statute has been implemented through the CEQ's regulations, which have provided clear direction to over 80 federal agencies, tribes, project sponsors, courts, impacted communities, and the broader public. The rescission of these regulations forces these entities to depend on agency-specific NEPA interpretations, which will cause confusion, delays, and litigation.

Concerningly, in guidance issued with the interim final rule, the CEQ urged agencies to use the controversial 2020 regulations issued during the first Trump administration, which were largely reversed by the Biden administration. These regulations were inconsistent with both the letter and spirit of the law; they undermined informed agency decision-making, reduced transparency, and limited critical public involvement, thus denying the public the democratic process at the heart of NEPA. Decisions on certain projects were allowed to move forward without full consideration of their environmental impacts and without a requirement that a broad range of safer, more ecologically sound alternatives be considered.

The interim final rule will cause NEPA processes to be more unpredictable, reducing the public's ability to fully raise concerns about the destruction of wildlife habitat and loss of biodiversity, declines in air and water quality, and harm to public health. I urge you to withdraw this rule.

comment:
Council on Environmental Quality
Docket number CEQ-2025-0002

Dear Acting Chair Scarlett:

I am strongly opposed to the interim final rule issued by the Council on Environmental Quality that will rescind 50 years' worth of regulations that implement the National Environmental Policy Act. This recission will upend established case law, policies and procedure and sow great uncertainty among federal agencies, industry, and local communities. I urge you to keep the current CEQ regulations in place.

NEPA was passed by Congress with overwhelming bipartisan support and signed into law by President Nixon in 1970. This statute is our country's basic charter for the protection of the environment, and one of the most important environmental laws in the United States. Since 1978, this vital statute has been implemented through the CEQ's regulations, which have provided clear direction to over 80 federal agencies, tribes, project sponsors, courts, impacted communities, and the broader public. The rescission of these regulations forces these entities to depend on agency-specific NEPA interpretations, which will cause confusion, delays, and litigation.

Concerningly, in guidance issued with the interim final rule, the CEQ urged agencies to use the controversial 2020 regulations issued during the first Trump administration, which were largely reversed by the Biden administration. These regulations were inconsistent with both the letter and spirit of the law; they undermined informed agency decision-making, reduced transparency, and limited critical public involvement, thus denying the public the democratic process at the heart of NEPA. Decisions on certain projects were allowed to move forward without full consideration of their environmental impacts and without a requirement that a broad range of safer, more ecologically sound alternatives be considered.

The interim final rule will cause NEPA processes to be more unpredictable, reducing the public's ability to fully raise concerns about the destruction of wildlife habitat and loss of biodiversity, declines in air and water quality, and harm to public health. I urge you to withdraw this rule.

comment:
Council on Environmental Quality
Docket number CEQ-2025-0002

Dear Acting Chair Scarlett:

I am strongly opposed to the interim final rule issued by the Council on Environmental Quality that will rescind 50 years' worth of regulations that implement the National Environmental Policy Act. This recission will upend established case law, policies and procedure and sow great uncertainty among federal agencies, industry, and local communities. I urge you to keep the current CEQ regulations in place.

NEPA was passed by Congress with overwhelming bipartisan support and signed into law by President Nixon in 1970. This statute is our country's basic charter for the protection of the environment, and one of the most important environmental laws in the United States. Since 1978, this vital statute has been implemented through the CEQ's regulations, which have provided clear direction to over 80 federal agencies, tribes, project sponsors, courts, impacted communities, and the broader public. The rescission of these regulations forces these entities to depend on agency-specific NEPA interpretations, which will cause confusion, delays, and litigation.

Concerningly, in guidance issued with the interim final rule, the CEQ urged agencies to use the controversial 2020 regulations issued during the first Trump administration, which were largely reversed by the Biden administration. These regulations were inconsistent with both the letter and spirit of the law; they undermined informed agency decision-making, reduced transparency, and limited critical public involvement, thus denying the public the democratic process at the heart of NEPA. comment:
Council on Environmental Quality
Docket number CEQ-2025-0002

Dear Acting Chair Scarlett:

I am strongly opposed to the interim final rule issued by the Council on Environmental Quality that will rescind 50 years' worth of regulations that implement the National Environmental Policy Act. This recission will upend established case law, policies and procedure and sow great uncertainty among federal agencies, industry, and local communities. I urge you to keep the current CEQ regulations in place.

NEPA was passed by Congress with overwhelming bipartisan support and signed into law by President Nixon in 1970. This statute is our country's basic charter for the protection of the environment, and one of the most important environmental laws in the United States. Since 1978, this vital statute has been implemented through the CEQ's regulations, which have provided clear direction to over 80 federal agencies, tribes, project sponsors, courts, impacted communities, and the broader public. The rescission of these regulations forces these entities to depend on agency-specific NEPA interpretations, which will cause confusion, delays, and litigation.

Concerningly, in guidance issued with the interim final rule, the CEQ urged agencies to use the controversial 2020 regulations issued during the first Trump administration, which were largely reversed by the Biden administration. These regulations were inconsistent with both the letter and spirit of the law; they undermined informed agency decision-making, reduced transparency, and limited critical public involvement, thus denying the public the democratic process at the heart of NEPA. Decisions on certain projects were allowed to move forward without full consideration of their environmental impacts and without a requirement that a broad range of safer, more ecologically sound alternatives be considered.

The interim final rule will cause NEPA processes to be more unpredictable, reducing the public's ability to fully raise concerns about the destruction of wildlife habitat and loss of biodiversity, declines in air and water quality, and harm to public health. I urge you to withdraw this rule.

comment:
I am writing to formally submit a public comment regarding the Council on Environmental Quality’s (CEQ) interim final rule to remove the existing National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) implementing regulations, as directed by Executive Order 14154, "Unleashing American Energy." As an environmental professional, I believe that NEPA should be applicable to discretionary decisions but should not be applicable to statutory decisions.

1. Distinguishing Between Discretionary and Statutory Decisions

NEPA’s purpose is to ensure that environmental considerations are adequately addressed in federal decision-making. However, its applicability should be limited to discretionary decisions where agencies have the authority to shape outcomes based on environmental impact assessments. Applying NEPA to statutory decisions—where agencies have little to no discretion—creates inefficiencies and unnecessary procedural burdens without meaningful environmental benefits.

For example, the 1872 Mining Law grants individuals and companies the statutory right to explore and extract minerals on public lands. Because the approval of mining operations under this law is a statutory obligation rather than a discretionary decision, requiring NEPA review adds procedural hurdles that do not influence the outcome. Federal agencies cannot deny a mining claim if all other statutory requirements are met, making the environmental review process redundant in many cases.

2. Reducing Unnecessary Delays for Statutory Decisions

When agencies are bound by statutory mandates, requiring NEPA reviews can lead to unnecessary delays and increased litigation risks. If an agency is legally required to take a specific action, an environmental review does not influence the outcome and merely adds bureaucratic hurdles. In contrast, discretionary decisions should remain subject to NEPA review, as agencies have the flexibility to incorporate environmental considerations into their decision-making.

3. Challenges of Applying NEPA to Mineral and Energy Projects

A core requirement of NEPA is the consideration of project alternatives, but for mineral and energy development projects, viable alternatives are often nonexistent. Unlike infrastructure projects where routes or locations can be modified to reduce impacts, mineral resources are geologically fixed. A mining or energy project cannot relocate to an area with fewer environmental impacts because the resource itself dictates the project location. As a result, NEPA’s alternative analysis requirement often serves as an unnecessary bureaucratic exercise rather than a meaningful planning tool for these types of projects.

4. Providing Clarity and Efficiency

A clear distinction between discretionary and statutory decisions will help streamline environmental reviews, ensuring that resources are allocated where they have the most impact. By refining NEPA’s scope, agencies can focus on substantive environmental protections rather than procedural redundancies. This approach would maintain the integrity of NEPA while preventing it from becoming an obstacle to legally mandated actions.

Conclusion

I urge CEQ to consider a more nuanced approach in its interim final rule by ensuring that NEPA applies to discretionary decisions while exempting statutory decisions, such as those governed by the 1872 Mining Law, from its procedural requirements. Additionally, for mineral and energy projects, the lack of viable alternatives should be recognized in NEPA processes to prevent unnecessary and impractical evaluations. This balanced approach would uphold NEPA’s original intent without imposing undue burdens on necessary government actions.

I appreciate the opportunity to submit this comment and encourage CEQ to carefully consider this distinction before finalizing its rule.

Council on Environmental Quality
Docket number CEQ-2025-0002

Dear Acting Chair Scarlett:

I am strongly opposed to the interim final rule issued by the Council on Environmental Quality that will rescind 50 years' worth of regulations that implement the National Environmental Policy Act. This recission will upend established case law, policies and procedure and sow great uncertainty among federal agencies, industry, and local communities. I urge you to keep the current CEQ regulations in place.

NEPA was passed by Congress with overwhelming bipartisan support and signed into law by President Nixon in 1970. This statute is our country's basic charter for the protection of the environment, and one of the most important environmental laws in the United States. Since 1978, this vital statute has been implemented through the CEQ's regulations, which have provided clear direction to over 80 federal agencies, tribes, project sponsors, courts, impacted communities, and the broader public. The rescission of these regulations forces these entities to depend on agency-specific NEPA interpretations, which will cause confusion, delays, and litigation.

Concerningly, in guidance issued with the interim final rule, the CEQ urged agencies to use the controversial 2020 regulations issued during the first Trump administration, which were largely reversed by the Biden administration. These regulations were inconsistent with both the letter and spirit of the law; they undermined informed agency decision-making, reduced transparency, and limited critical public involvement, thus denying the public the democratic process at the heart of NEPA. Decisions on certain projects were allowed to move forward without full consideration of their environmental impacts and without a requirement that a broad range of safer, more ecologically sound alternatives be considered.

The interim final rule will cause NEPA processes to be more unpredictable, reducing the public's ability to fully raise concerns about the destruction of wildlife habitat and loss of biodiversity, declines in air and water quality, and harm to public health. I urge you to withdraw this rule.

comment:
Introduction
The Council on Environmental Quality (CEG) has long played a crucial role in ensuring federal agencies follow consistent, science-based processes when evaluating environmental impacts under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA). Revoking these regulations creates unnecessary uncertainty, weakens public participation, and erodes environmental protections, undermining the very purpose of NEPA to provide transparency and accountability in federal decision-making. In addition, contrary to this Administration's intentions, revoking decades-old rules that have since become industry best practices will only add more time, money, and complexity to the permitting process in the foreseeable future. Doesn't sound too efficient, does it?

Background & Analysis
NEPA requires federal agencies to create a "detailed statement" for "major Federal actions significantly affecting the quality of the human environment." Under NEPA, the CEQ is in charge of assisting and advising the President on such matters. Executive Order 11991, which has been in effect since 1978, gave CEQ the authority to be the primary rulemaking body under NEPA for other federal agencies to follow. If this Administration wants to rescind CEQ's invaluable NEPA guidance to "unleash American energy" so that "important" projects can get approved sooner, perhaps the Administration needs a couple of reminders on the unintended consequences of this decision on issues they deem to "care" about.
1. Property Rights: Landowners, ranch owners, and small business owners will be negatively impacted by this recension. NEPA provides them a voice in the project planning process. Without the opportunity to make their voice heard, rural communities (many of whom voted for this Administration) will risk having their lands swept up--even more than they already have been in the past--by oil and gas projects.
2. Investor Confidence: Investors want stability and assurance. Removing NEPA from the equation does this exact opposite by opening up projects to even more legal challenges in the future. If this Administration wants investors to pump their money into the American economy, then this revocation just shows that the Administration simply doesn't understand the investment landscape of today's times.
3. Government Overreach: This Administration will try to argue that NEPA is a form of government overreach. In reality, though, NEPA is a way for local communities to make their voices heard in the face of large-scale developments on and near their lands. Without NEPA, federal agencies will push forward projects without a care in the world for what happens to local communities. I'd choose NEPA's form of "government overreach" anytime.
4. Reducing Costs/Time: Related to the second point, NEPA ensures that projects are legally sound from the eyes of the federal government. Without NEPA's stamp of approval, investors and developers run the risk of getting caught up in costly legal fees that would in turn potentially stall production on their projects for years at a time. This is common-sense, basic preemptive risk management.

Conclusion
Do away with this interim final rule. Other voters may have thought they were electing a conservative Administration to the White House, but as I've laid out here, this decision does not reflect their conservative values. It reflects fascist values that conservatives and progressives can both agree that we oppose. This Administration does not care about the people who voted for it, and it is grossly apparent in this interim final rule and Executive Order 14154. This Administration cares about consolidating more and more power under a single, radical ideology that seeks to bypass institutional checks and balances, like NEPA, that are there for a reason, to serve their own interests. NEPA is for the broader public good--let's keep it that way.

comment:
Council on Environmental Quality
Docket number CEQ-2025-0002

Dear Acting Chair Scarlett:

I am strongly opposed to the interim final rule issued by the Council on Environmental Quality that will rescind 50 years' worth of regulations that implement the National Environmental Policy Act. This recission will upend established case law, policies and procedure and sow great uncertainty among federal agencies, industry, and local communities. I urge you to keep the current CEQ regulations in place.

NEPA was passed by Congress with overwhelming bipartisan support and signed into law by President Nixon in 1970. This statute is our country's basic charter for the protection of the environment, and one of the most important environmental laws in the United States. Since 1978, this vital statute has been implemented through the CEQ's regulations, which have provided clear direction to over 80 federal agencies, tribes, project sponsors, courts, impacted communities, and the broader public. The rescission of these regulations forces these entities to depend on agency-specific NEPA interpretations, which will cause confusion, delays, and litigation.

Concerningly, in guidance issued with the interim final rule, the CEQ urged agencies to use the controversial 2020 regulations issued during the first Trump administration, which were largely reversed by the Biden administration. These regulations were inconsistent with both the letter and spirit of the law; they undermined informed agency decision-making, reduced transparency, and limited critical public involvement, thus denying the public the democratic process at the heart of NEPA. Decisions on certain projects were allowed to move forward without full consideration of their environmental impacts and without a requirement that a broad range of safer, more ecologically sound alternatives be considered.

The interim final rule will cause NEPA processes to be more unpredictable, reducing the public's ability to fully raise concerns about the destruction of wildlife habitat and loss of biodiversity, declines in air and water quality, and harm to public health. I urge you to withdraw this rule.
